item.text:
**4B.6 Research Note**

Overall read: **mostly yes, with real caveats**. In 2024 Lula’s government showed more openness than Bolsonaro-era Brazil in its posture toward the press and information access: official speech archives were published, social-media blocks from the prior administration were reversed, and reporting on journalists suggests a somewhat less hostile environment. The main counterevidence is that the government and courts still pressed hard on misinformation and platform compliance, which can create chill even if it is framed as anti-disinformation.

- [Onde posso acessar discurso e pronunciamentos do Presidente da República Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva?](https://www.gov.br/secom/pt-br/acesso-a-informacao/perguntas-frequentes/onde-posso-acessar-discurso-e) — Secretaria de Comunicação Social — 2024-03-21 — The government pointed the public to official transcripts, audio, and video archives for Lula’s speeches. That is a concrete transparency measure supporting information access rather than secrecy or propaganda. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.5`

- [Brazil | Digital News Report 2024](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2024/brazil) — Reuters Institute — 2024-06-17 — The report says the “fake news” bill was abandoned and that Brazil still has trusted mainstream outlets, despite strong polarization and misinformation pressures. This supports a relatively open media environment under Lula, even though it does not eliminate pressure concerns. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.3` `4B.5` `4B.2`

- [Brazil | Freedom in the World 2024 Country Report](https://freedomhouse.org/country/brazil/freedom-world/2024) — Freedom House — 2024 — Freedom House says Brazil has a vibrant, competitive media and public debate, and specifically notes that the Lula administration has not maintained the Bolsonaro-era practice of monitoring public servants for criticism. This is strong evidence for a less coercive information environment. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.3` `4B.5`

- [Brazil | Freedom on the Net 2024 Country Report](https://freedomhouse.org/country/brazil/freedom-net/2024) — Freedom House — 2024 — Freedom House says online journalists and users generally face a somewhat less restrictive environment under Lula than under Bolsonaro, even though legal threats and harassment still exist. That is supportive, but not a full clean bill of health. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.3` `4B.5`

- [Brazil | Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2024/brazil) — Reuters Institute — 2024-06-17 — The report says attacks on journalists fell by 52% to 181 in 2024, while warning that threats and legal restrictions still remain part of the picture. This is one of the best quantitative signs that the Lula-era environment was less hostile than before. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.3`

- [Em 2024, jornalistas sofreram uma agressão a cada 2 dias e meio no Brasil, aponta relatório da FENAJ](https://www.abi.org.br/em-2024-jornalistas-sofreram-uma-agressao-a-cada-2-dias-e-meio-no-brasil-aponta-relatorio-da-fenaj/) — ABI / FENAJ — 2024-05-20 — FENAJ reported 144 attacks on journalists in 2024, down from 181 in 2023, but still a severe problem. This supports a mixed verdict: conditions improved somewhat, but intimidation and violence against media did not disappear. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.3`

- [Brazil: Mixed Rights Record for Lula’s First Year](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/01/11/brazil-mixed-rights-record-lulas-first-year) — Human Rights Watch — 2024-01-11 — HRW said Lula made important progress on rights, and later noted that his government unblocked more than 3,000 social-media users previously blocked from institutional accounts under Bolsonaro. That is a concrete pro-access move. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.3` `4B.5`

- [Brazil | World Report 2024](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/brazil) — Human Rights Watch — 2024 — HRW repeated that the government announced it would unblock more than 3,000 users from Bolsonaro-era institutional account blocks, which is a direct reversal of prior restrictions and favorable for information access. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.3`

- [Youtube retira do ar desinformação sobre estado de saúde do presidente da República](https://www.gov.br/agu/pt-br/comunicacao/noticias/youtube-retira-do-ar-desinformacao-sobre-estado-de-saude-do-presidente-da-republica/) — Advocacia-Geral da União — 2024-12-16 — The AGU pushed YouTube to remove videos spreading false claims about Lula’s health. This is the clearest counterevidence: it shows active state pressure on information flow, though it was framed as anti-disinformation rather than direct censorship of legitimate journalism. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.2` `4B.5`

- [Brazil | Digital News Report 2025](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2025/brazil) — Reuters Institute — 2025, covering 2024 events — The report describes Brazil’s platform-regulation and misinformation battles, including a January 2024 false-tax rumor that forced the government to withdraw a regulation package. This is the strongest broader caveat: Lula’s environment still pressured information flows, even if the pressure was not always directly anti-press. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.2` `4B.5`

- [X has been blocked in Brazil. Does it matter for journalism?](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/news/x-has-been-blocked-brazil-does-it-matter-journalism) — Reuters Institute — 2024-09-16 — The article describes Brazil’s Supreme Court blocking X after noncompliance with legal orders, with journalists split on whether it was lawful enforcement or a free-speech problem. This is a real chill-risk caveat for information access, but it is not clear Lula-directed retaliation against journalists. Question IDs: `4B.6` `4B.2` `4B.3` `4B.5`

Search gap: I did **not** find strong 2024 evidence that Lula personally pressured owners or journalists in the style of Bolsonaro. The negatives I found are mostly institutional and indirect: misinformation enforcement, platform rules, and court actions. The strongest positive evidence is transparency and reversal of Bolsonaro-era restrictions, but the media environment remained polarized and litigated.
